newsitem.title: USA: Senate committee passes baseball antitrust bill.
newsitem.headline: Senate committee passes baseball antitrust bill.

text.p: The Senate Judiciary Committee voted 11-6 Thursday for a bill to lift part of baseball's antitrust exemption and make it play by the same labour rules as other professional sports.

The bill would only apply to major leagues, not the minors. It reflected language acceptable to league owners and players after negotiations that were an outgrowth of the collective bargaining agreement signed last year.

"Approval of this bill is a major victory for baseball fans," said Judiciary Chairman Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican who has pushed for this measure since a players strike led to the cancellation of the 1994 World Series.
"It will bring about sound reforms that ensure that baseball remains strong and is treated fairly and properly under the antitrust laws," Hatch said.

It would lift baseball's 75-year-old antitrust exemption on labour laws, which among other things prevents players from lodging unfair labour practices complaints with the National Labour Relations Board. Other pro sports do not have that exemption.
The bill would not affect franchise relocation rules or affect team's power to negotiate collectively and share revenue from television rights.

The bill is named for the late Curt Flood, a star outfielder with the St. Louis Cardinals who jeopardised his career by challenging baseball's reserve clause 25 years ago. Although that bid failed, his action paved the way for eliminating baseball's reserve clause a few years later and letting players move from team to team as free agents.
